title.rendered: Vermonters to Vote on Equal Protection Amendment to State Constitution

excerpt.rendered: Vermont voters will have the chance to weigh in on another amendment to the state’s constitution this fall. content.rendered:
Vermont voters will have the chance to weigh in on another amendment to the state’s constitution this fall. The proposal, which received final approval from the House in May 2026, is aimed at ensuring all people are treated equally under the law regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or national origin.

A statewide vote is the last step in the yearslong process that Proposal 4 — also known as PR.4 — must follow before it can become part of Vermont’s founding document. The Senate gave its final legislative sign-off in March 2026, and the measure will appear on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot.

What would Proposal 4 change?

If approved by a majority of voters, the amendment would add Article 23 to Chapter I of the Vermont Constitution. The new provision would guarantee equal protection under the law and state that Vermont “shall not deny equal treatment under the law” based on nine protected characteristics:

  • Race
  • Ethnicity
  • Sex
  • Religion
  • Disability
  • Sexual orientation
  • Gender identity
  • Gender expression
  • National origin

The proposed text also clarifies that the amendment would not prevent the state from adopting measures intended to provide equality of treatment and opportunity for groups that have historically faced discrimination.

Supporters describe the measure as building on the U.S. Constitution’s 14th Amendment equal protection clause by explicitly naming groups that have historically experienced discrimination in Vermont and across the country. If enacted, it would become the 23rd article of the state constitution and could form the basis of future Vermont Supreme Court decisions involving civil rights and government policy.

How did the amendment reach the ballot?

Constitutional amendments in Vermont must pass both chambers of the Legislature in two separate biennia before they can be placed before voters. Proposal 4 was first advanced by the Senate nearly a decade ago and has moved through the Statehouse with broad bipartisan support during its most recent legislative sessions.

In 2024, the Senate approved the measure unanimously and the House passed it with only a handful of dissenting votes. Lawmakers completed the second round of approval in 2026, clearing the way for the public vote this fall.

Vermont is among a minority of states that do not already include an equal protection or equal rights clause in their state constitutions. Civil rights advocates have pushed for the change for decades, and momentum increased after a series of U.S. Supreme Court decisions that narrowed federal protections in areas such as reproductive rights and anti-discrimination law.

A recent history of constitutional change in Vermont

If voters approve Proposal 4, it would be the third change to the Vermont Constitution in four years. In 2022, Vermonters overwhelmingly passed amendments that:

  • Explicitly prohibited slavery and indentured servitude under the state constitution
  • Broadly protected reproductive health care decisions, including abortion, from state interference

This fall’s vote comes nearly 40 years after Vermonters narrowly rejected a different equal-rights proposal. In 1986, an amendment focused specifically on guaranteeing equal treatment on the basis of sex failed with just under 52% opposed — even though the federal Equal Rights Amendment had not been ratified by enough states to take effect nationally.

Why health policy watchers are paying attention

Although Proposal 4 is not a health care bill, constitutional equal-protection language can influence how courts and regulators interpret state rules — including rules that affect health insurance and access to care.

For example, explicit protections related to disability, sex, gender identity, and sexual orientation can reinforce state-level safeguards that overlap with federal requirements under the Affordable Care Act (ACA), including Marketplace anti-discrimination rules and regulations implementing ACA Section 1557.

Vermont already has a reputation as one of the more progressive states on health coverage policy. The state operates its own health insurance Marketplace, expanded Medicaid under the ACA, and — like several other states — does not allow short-term limited-duration health plans to be sold to residents.

Still, supporters argue that embedding equal treatment principles directly in the state constitution provides stronger, longer-lasting protection than statutes or agency rules alone — particularly if federal policy shifts over time.

What happens after the November vote?

Proposal 4 needs a simple majority to pass. If approved, the amendment would take effect after certification of the election results, in accordance with Vermont’s constitutional amendment procedures.

Opponents have raised concerns about how courts might interpret the amendment in future cases, while supporters emphasize that the measure reflects values already expressed elsewhere in the Vermont Constitution — including declarations that all people are born equally free and that government exists for the common benefit and security of the people.

For now, the decision rests with voters. Between now and November 3, 2026, advocacy groups on both sides are expected to make their case to Vermonters about whether explicit constitutional equal protection language belongs in the state’s founding document.

Louise Norris is an individual health insurance broker who has been writing about health insurance and health reform since 2006. She has written dozens of opinions and educational pieces about the Affordable Care Act for healthinsurance.org.
